summary: This paper experimentally demonstrates layered error suppression in fiber-interconnected superconducting quantum processors using a quantum collisional model to emulate transduction and fiber noise on IBM's 156-qubit Heron r2 device. The combined application of entanglement purification (BBPSSW protocol), Pauli twirling, and readout mitigation recovers remote CNOT fidelity by over 20% in the high-noise regime, with Bell-state fidelity improving from ∼0.42 to ∼0.63 at 10 fiber steps.
motivation: Distributed quantum computing via interconnected QPUs requires high-fidelity remote gates, but communication-induced noise from transduction and fiber links degrades entanglement quality and gate performance; systematic experimental quantification of error mitigation effectiveness under realistic distributed noise was lacking.
method: Bell pairs distributed between remote communication qubits are subjected to controlled communication noise via sequential interactions with environment ancillae (collisional model with coupling strength κ emulating G.652-D fiber at α=0.0145 km⁻¹ and transduction loss). Error suppression combines entanglement purification via LOCC with probabilistic post-selection, Pauli-twirled two-qubit gates executed via cat-state protocol, and readout mitigation with inverted assignment matrices, tested on IBM ibm_kingston with 10,000 shots per circuit.
result: Baseline remote CNOT fidelity degrades from ∼0.97 to <0.50 across 10 fiber steps; entanglement purification alone restores fidelity to ∼0.63 (>20% improvement), with purification dominant over Pauli twirling (~5% gain) at high noise; the full three-layer approach achieves success probabilities of ∼0.58–0.62 at step 10.
